title: Rebranding without confusing the people who already buy
excerpt: Rebrand when the offer or the audience changed, not when the team is bored of the old site. Keep the paths regulars already use while the surface changes.
alt: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass. The sign in the window fits a piece about changing the surface without confusing people who already know the door.
caption: Regulars still need to recognize the door. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a startup rebrand?
faqs.answer: When the offer changed, or the audience changed, and the old name, look, or language now misleads people. Boredom with the site, a new hire's taste, or a competitor's launch are weak reasons. A refresh of type and color can wait for a real change in the company.

faqs.question: How do you rebrand without losing current customers?
faqs.answer: Keep the name if it is still true. Keep the URLs and the paths people already use. Say what changed in one plain sentence, in the places regulars will see it, such as the homepage and the email they already receive. Do not make them relearn how to buy, log in, or contact you in the same week you change the logo.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a rebrand and a redesign?
faqs.answer: A redesign can change the structure and the craft of a site while the company stays the same. A rebrand changes what the company claims to be: the name, the audience, or the offer. Many teams need a redesign, and fewer need a new identity. Doing both at once raises the chance that regulars feel lost.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Decide when to rebrand a startup by asking whether the offer or the audience changed. If they did, the old name or the old surface may be telling a lie. If they did not, and the team is simply bored, a rebrand will spend trust that regulars already extended to you. Change the work that is failing. Leave the recognition alone.

People who already buy from you are not a segment to surprise. They know the door, the name, and the path to pay or log in. A new look can be welcome. A new puzzle is not. The work is to change the surface without moving the door.

## Reasons that are real

The offer changed. You sold a single report, and you now sell the tool that produces it. The old name describes the report so narrowly that the new buyer, and the old one, misunderstand what you are. A rebrand here is a correction.

The audience changed. You started with hobbyists and the buyers are now operators of a business, or the reverse. The tone, the proof, and the pictures are aimed at someone who no longer arrives. Keeping the old costume makes the new conversation harder than it needs to be.

The name became false or unusable. It collided with a company people confuse with you. It described a feature you removed. It cannot be said on a phone. Those are structural problems. A new coat of paint on the website will not fix them.

Thomas Bewick, a heritage craft brand with an editorial site, is a useful picture of the opposite case. The craft was the point. The site had to become modern without pretending the company was a different kind of company. That is a redesign in service of recognition, which is not the same project as a rebrand.

## Reasons that are boredom

The founder has looked at the homepage too many times. A new designer wants a portfolio piece. A competitor launched a fashionable site. None of these mean your buyers are confused. They mean you are restless.

Restlessness can still justify a careful visual refresh: type, spacing, a photograph that matches the offer you already have. Call it a refresh. Do not rename the company, rewrite the offer into abstraction, and move every URL because the team wanted a moment.

Google's page on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is a good conscience check for the words you are about to change. The question is whether the page helps a person who came to you directly, and whether the heading describes the page without exaggeration. A rebrand that replaces a clear offer with a louder claim is search-engine theater and customer theater at the same time. The regulars notice first.

## What regulars need you to keep

Keep the name unless the name is the problem. Recognition lives there more than in the color. If the name stays, say so in the first screen, in the old words, before you introduce the new ones. We are still {name}. We now do {the changed offer}.

Keep the paths. The login URL, the pricing URL, the address of the page they bookmarked, the email they reply to. If a URL must change, redirect it. Do not ask a customer to relearn the route in the same week the logo moves. Google's notes on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) are a reminder that the visible title of a result should describe the page, and that outdated or inaccurate titles get replaced by other text on the page anyway. After a rebrand, check the title and the heading of every page you kept. A title that still describes last year's offer will confuse searchers and regulars with the same sentence.

Keep the proof they already believed. A customer list, a product they use, a story they recognize. You can design it better. Removing it because the new brand is too elevated for specifics is how you look like you were acquired by a company that does not know them.

Keep a way to ask a person. The contact path should be as obvious as before, or more obvious. A rebrand that hides the email behind a new concept site is a rebrand that tells regulars the relationship was decorative.

## How to change the surface

Write one sentence about what changed and put it where regulars will see it. The homepage, the receipt email, the login screen. Do not write a manifesto with a countdown. A countdown is pressure. The news is a sentence.

Change the system, not a single hero image. If the type, the color, and the sentence update together, the product and the site still feel like one company. If only the homepage campaign changes, you have a poster sitting on top of the old product, and the seam shows at login.

Stage the new site and click the paths a regular uses. Buy, log in, find a document, reply. Do this before the public switch. The unglamorous bugs are the ones that make a rebrand feel like a breakup: a broken bookmark, a logo that 404s in an old email, a help doc that still uses the retired name in a way that sounds like a different product.

For a while, answer to both names if the name changed. In the inbox, in the support macro, in the footer. Retire the old name when the mail actually slows, not on the morning of the announcement because the guidelines say the old name is forbidden.

## What to postpone

Postpone a new name if a new sentence would do. Many teams can say the new offer under the old name and keep every relationship they have. A name change is a last tool, because it spends the recognition you already paid for.

Postpone a simultaneous rebuild of the product interface unless the interface is part of the lie. Doing a rebrand, a replatform, and a new information architecture in one launch multiplies the ways a regular can get lost. Sequence them. Surface first, with paths stable. Structure next, with redirects. Product language once the words are settled.

If you are unsure which kind of change you need, start with trust rather than with a blank page. [How to redesign without losing people who already trust you](/blog/redesign-without-losing-trust) is the next piece. It stays with the paths and the offer regulars already understand.

When a real change in the offer is forcing the question, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) and bring the old sentence and the new one. The useful outcome is whether you need a new identity or a clearer page.
